title: Karanj (Pongamia) Chewing Stick: A Natural Toothbrush Twig
excerpt: Karanj datun is a pongam twig chewed into a natural toothbrush. What studies show, how chewing sticks like miswak work, and why fluoride still matters.
content:
Quick answer: Karanj datun is a fresh twig of the pongam tree (Pongamia pinnata, also listed as Millettia pinnata) that people in India chew into a soft brush and use to clean their teeth. It belongs to a worldwide tradition of chewing sticks, the best known being miswak from the Arak tree in the Middle East and Africa. Lab studies show karanj extracts have only mild activity against a key tooth-decay bacterium. A twig can scrub plaque off your teeth, but it delivers no fluoride, so dentists and health bodies still recommend brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste.

If you grew up in New York or Manchester, brushing your teeth with a stick probably sounds like something from a history book. In much of India it is an ordinary morning: snap a young twig from a neem, babool or karanj tree, chew one end until it frays, and scrub.

What is a datun, or chewing stick?

"Datun" is the everyday Hindi word for a tooth-cleaning twig. A 2026 study by dental researchers in Bihar describes datun as still widely used in rural India, and notes that chewing sticks are among the oldest known ways of removing plaque by hand.

The idea is far older than India's villages. A 2012 review in the Saudi Dental Journal traces chewing sticks to the Babylonians around 3500 BC and says they are still used for cleaning teeth across Asia, Africa, South America and the Middle East. At least 182 plant species can be made into one. The most studied is miswak, Arabic for "tooth-cleaning stick," which comes from the Arak tree (Salvadora persica). That tree grows from Rajasthan and Nepal through Iran, Arabia and Egypt to Mauritania, and south through Sudan and Ethiopia.

According to the same review, the World Health Organization's 2000 consensus report on oral hygiene said chewing sticks may play a role in promoting oral hygiene and that their effectiveness deserves further study. That is a call for more research, and it does not rank sticks above toothbrushes.

What is the karanj tree?

Karanj is the Hindi name for the pongam tree, known in English as Indian beech or pongam oil tree. Kew's Plants of the World Online lists the accepted name as Pongamia pinnata (L.) Pierre, in the legume family Fabaceae. Its native range runs from tropical and subtropical Asia to the western Pacific, mainly in the seasonally dry tropics, and it is rated Least Concern for extinction risk.

FeatureDetails

The Indian names come from India Flora Online, run by the herbarium at the Indian Institute of Science. In Ayurveda, India's traditional medical system, karanja appears as a remedy for skin and other complaints. James Duke's Handbook of Energy Crops (1983), hosted by Purdue University, records that its twigs are used as chewsticks and its roots for cleaning the gums and teeth.

How do you recognize a karanj tree?

The World Agroforestry tree database gives the clearest description. Look for:

  • Compound leaves with 5 to 9 glossy leaflets, all paired except one at the tip. New leaves are pinkish red and turn dark green.
  • Drooping clusters of small, scented flowers that look like pea blossoms, white to pink with purple inside.
  • Flat, thick-walled, woody pods about 3 to 8 cm long that hold one or two bean-like seeds and do not split open on their own.
  • Smooth, gray-brown bark.

You are putting this plant in your mouth, so if you are unsure of the tree, skip it.

Does a karanj chewing stick actually clean teeth?

Mostly through scrubbing. The Saudi review concludes that miswak's value comes chiefly from its mechanical cleaning action, with extra saliva from chewing also playing a part. Karanj twigs presumably work the same way, but we could not find a clinical trial of karanj datun itself.

The antibacterial evidence for karanj is thin. In the 2026 study published in Bioinformation, researchers in Patna dried mango and karanj twigs, soaked the powder in water, and tested the extracts against Streptococcus mutans, a main cause of tooth decay. At 5% strength neither extract stopped the bacteria. At 50%, karanj produced a 1.8 mm zone of inhibition after 48 hours, against 2.7 mm for mango. The authors ran no statistical tests and concluded mango was the stronger of the two.

A 2018 study in Pharmacognosy Magazine from the University of Pretoria found something similar. It tested ethanol extracts of karanj leaves against S. mutans and found no significant antibacterial activity, with effects appearing only at the highest concentration tested. Mango and neem did better. Older lab work found the seed oil inhibits several bacteria. None of this comes from human trials.

What compounds are in karanj?

The plant contains several flavonoids. The best known is karanjin, which a 2026 paper in Toxicology Reports describes as a benzofuran flavonoid from the seeds. Duke's handbook also lists pongamol, pongapin, kanjone, pinnatin, kaempferol, quercetin, saponins, beta-sitosterol and tannins.

The oil comes from the seeds. A 2011 analysis in the Journal of the American Oil Chemists' Society found oleic acid to be the main fatty acid, along with a notable amount of erucic acid.

How do you use a chewing stick?

Most published instructions are for miswak, but they carry over to other twigs. A 2015 article from the Murdoch Children's Research Institute in Melbourne describes the method: soften the stick, remove the outer bark at one end, then chew that end until it frays into a brush. The basic steps:

  1. Pick a fresh, young twig from a tree you have identified with confidence.
  2. Wash it well in clean water.
  3. Peel the bark from one end and chew it gently until the fibers spread into bristles.
  4. Brush gently along the outer and inner surfaces of your teeth. Do not scrub hard at the gum line.
  5. Spit out the fibers and any juice. Do not swallow them.
  6. Rinse your mouth, then throw the used end away. Use a fresh piece next time.
  7. Never share a chewing stick. The FDI World Dental Federation advises against sharing even toothbrushes.

Technique has limits. The Saudi review notes that because a stick's bristles run along its length, the inner surfaces of the teeth are hard to reach. Users may also over-scrub the front teeth and miss the back ones, and studies have linked excessive miswak use to receding gums.

Is karanj safe to put in your mouth?

The twig has a long history of use. The seeds and oil are another matter. Duke's handbook states plainly that pongam oil and the residue left after pressing are toxic, and that the seeds have been used to poison fish. The 2011 oil study found that the erucic acid and toxic flavonoids, including karanjin, pongapin and pongaglabrin, make the seed oil inedible under WHO recommendations. The World Agroforestry database adds that the pressed seed cake is bitter and contains toxic factors, chiefly karanjin, pongamol and tannin.

The picture on karanjin alone is more complicated. The 2026 Toxicology Reports study gave purified karanjin to rats for up to 28 days and found no deaths or organ damage. That tells you about one isolated compound in rats. It does not make the seeds or oil safe to eat.

Practical precautions:

  • Use only the twig. Never chew, eat or swallow the seeds, and do not take the seed oil by mouth.
  • Spit out the juice and fibers rather than swallowing them.
  • Stop if you notice burning, a rash, swelling or sore gums, and see a dentist or doctor if it persists.
  • Supervise children closely. The UK's NHS says children need help or supervision with toothbrushing until they are at least 7.
  • Do not treat a chewing stick as a replacement for dental checkups or treatment.

Can karanj replace your toothbrush and toothpaste?

No. Fluoride is the part a twig cannot provide. As of November 2026, WHO's oral health fact sheet says twice-daily brushing with fluoride toothpaste at 1,000 to 1,500 ppm should be encouraged, and it calls adequate fluoride exposure essential for preventing tooth decay. WHO estimates that oral diseases affect nearly 3.7 billion people.

The NHS advises adults to brush twice a day for about two minutes with a toothpaste containing at least 1,350 ppm fluoride, then spit without rinsing. The American Dental Association tells patients to brush twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, clean between their teeth daily, and see a dentist regularly. The FDI World Dental Federation recommends brushing last thing at night and at least one other time each day.

If karanj datun is part of your family's routine, keep it as an extra alongside fluoride toothpaste.

Why do people grow the karanj tree?

Mostly for reasons that have nothing to do with teeth. It is one of the few nitrogen-fixing trees whose seeds carry oil, according to World Agroforestry. Its roots form nodules with soil bacteria that pull nitrogen from the air. India Flora Online notes the seeds are gaining popularity as a biofuel source, and the 2011 oil study found properties that suit biodiesel.

The tree is also planted for shade along roads, canals and pastures. In India its flowers are considered a good source of pollen and nectar for honeybees. It grows best in deep, well-drained sandy loam, does well in full sun and tolerates salty soils. Growers raise it from directly sown seed, root suckers or branch cuttings.

One caution for gardeners: World Agroforestry warns that its spreading roots and many suckers can make it a weed if left unmanaged.

Health disclaimer: This article is for general information and is not medical or dental advice. We found no clinical trials of karanj chewing sticks, and they are not a proven treatment for tooth decay or gum disease. Karanj seeds and seed oil should not be eaten. Talk to a dentist before changing your oral care routine, especially for children or if you have gum problems. Research details are accurate as of November 2026.

FAQ

What does "datun" mean?

Datun is a Hindi word for a tooth-cleaning twig, chewed at one end until it frays into a brush. Neem, babool, mango and karanj are common choices in India.

Is karanj the same as miswak?

No. Both are chewing sticks, but miswak comes from the Arak tree (Salvadora persica), while karanj comes from the pongam tree (Pongamia pinnata). Miswak has been studied far more.

Does a karanj datun kill cavity-causing bacteria?

Only weakly, and only in the lab. In a 2026 study a strong karanj extract held back Streptococcus mutans a little, less than mango did, and a weak one had no effect. We found no human trial.

Can I swallow the juice from a karanj twig?

It is best not to. Spit out the juice and fibers. Never eat karanj seeds or drink the seed oil, which researchers describe as toxic and inedible.

Should I stop using fluoride toothpaste if I use a chewing stick?

No. WHO, the NHS and the American Dental Association all recommend brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste. A chewing stick does not supply fluoride.

Can children use karanj datun?

Only with close adult supervision, and never in place of a toothbrush with fluoride toothpaste. The NHS says children need help or supervision with brushing until at least age 7.
